issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette: Kofi had always been a man who took pride in his community, working at the local retail store and volunteering at the nearby church. But that all changed when Hurricane Katrina devastated their small town in Louisiana. Kofi's family was forced to evacuate, leaving behind their home and business. The memories of that fateful day still lingered, like an open wound. As Kofi recalled the event, he felt like it was happening all over again - the howling wind, the sound of shattering glass, the feeling of helplessness as they watched their neighborhood being ravaged by floodwaters. These memories replayed in his mind like a film on repeat, making him feel like he was still trapped in that moment. He couldn't shake off the feeling that the world was a dangerous place, and that he had permanently changed for the worse. Kofi's wife, Ama, noticed a change in him too. He would constantly scan their surroundings, checking for exits and potential threats, even in the comfort of their own home. At night, Kofi would lie awake, vigilant, as if waiting for another disaster to strike. His hypervigilance had become exhausting, but he couldn't seem to shake it off. When Ama asked him why he was so on edge all the time, Kofi simply replied that he needed to be prepared - after all, the world was a treacherous place. As time passed, Kofi's behaviors became more pronounced. He would distract himself with work or TV to avoid thinking about the hurricane, but it only seemed to push the memories further down, making them resurface in his dreams. At the store where he worked, Kofi made sure to stay close to the exit, always keeping an eye on the door, just in case. His coworkers noticed his constant scanning of the surroundings and began to wonder if he was okay. One day, while restocking shelves, Kofi caught himself thinking about the hurricane again. He felt a wave of anxiety wash over him, and suddenly, the store's fluorescent lights seemed too bright, the noise too loud. He quickly excused himself and stepped outside for some fresh air, feeling overwhelmed by the sense of threat that lingered in every corner. Ama had been urging him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant - what if he wasn't strong enough to face his fears? Lately, however, Kofi's avoidance behaviors have started to take a toll on his relationships and work performance. He feels like he's losing himself in the process of trying to stay safe. His wife is worried about him, and his manager has mentioned that his constant distractions are affecting his job. It's this growing sense of unease that finally brought Kofi to seek help - he wants to learn how to live with his memories without letting them control his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kofi couldn't help but scan the room for exits, a habit he knew was hard to break. But with each passing minute, he felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to let go of the past and find a way to heal.
